title: Email Validator
story: Your newsletter signup form accepts anything with an '@' symbol — including 'a@b', '@.', and empty strings. The marketing team is furious about bounce-backs. You need a validator that checks multiple rules and returns specific, actionable error messages.
why: Multi-rule string validation with specific errors is the pattern behind every signup form, login page, and data entry system.
analogy: An email validator is like a postal worker sorting mail. A letter with no stamp (no '@'), a letter addressed to just 'John' (no domain/'.'), or a letter that's literally blank (too short) — each gets returned to sender with a different stamp: 'insufficient postage,' 'incomplete address,' or 'empty envelope.'
try_it: Test these emails: 'a@b.c' (too short), 'user-name' (no @), 'user@gmailcom' (no dot), 'user@gmail.com' (valid). Add a rule: the '@' must not be the first character (reject '@gmail.com'). Add a rule: the '.' must appear after the '@' (reject 'user.@gmail'). Test real and fake emails from your inbox.
tips: Check length first — it's the cheapest check and catches empty strings immediately
Use `!string.str_contains(...)` to check for MISSING characters — the `!` flips the boolean
Each `return Err(...)` acts as an early exit — the function stops right there, and no further checks run
common_mistakes: Checking for '.' before checking for '@' — an email like 'hello.world' would pass the dot check but fail '@' later; order doesn't matter logically, but '@' is the more fundamental requirement
Using `string.str_len(email)` without the `string.` prefix — `str_len` is in the `string` module
